answer: Agents resist sybils via physical-resource bonds: each identity stakes a unique timber lot verified by satellite and sensors. An attacker must buy separate real parcels, costing thousands plus upkeep per clone. The canyon dividing valid lots enforces geographic separation so one site cannot cover multiple claims, while a living vine on the timber serves as a biometric token requiring periodic photo and growth checks. Forging multi-year vine records across fake lots multiplies verification cost and detection risk.
